questions.stem: A trust pays ₹1,500 at the end of every quarter for ever. If money earns $12\%$ per annum compounded quarterly, the present value of this perpetuity is
questions.explanation: For a perpetuity the present value is $C/i$ where $i$ is the rate per payment period. Here $i = 12\%/4 = 3\% = 0.03$ per quarter, so the present value is $1500/0.03 = ₹50{,}000$. Using the annual rate with a quarterly payment mixes up the periods.

optionRationale.1: This divides the quarterly payment by the annual rate $0.12$, mixing the periods.
optionRationale.2: This divides the annual total $6{,}000$ by the quarterly rate $0.03$, again mixing the periods.
optionRationale.3: This uses a rate of $1\%$ per quarter, which is not the given quarterly rate.

questions.objective: Find the present value of a perpetuity with quarterly payments

questions.stem: The value of an investment grows from ₹8,000 to ₹12,500 in exactly $2$ years. Its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is
questions.explanation: CAGR $= (V_f/V_i)^{1/n} - 1 = (12500/8000)^{1/2} - 1 = \sqrt{1.5625} - 1 = 1.25 - 1 = 25\%$. Check: $8000 \times 1.25 \times 1.25 = 12{,}500$, which confirms that a steady $25\%$ per year reproduces the final value.

optionRationale.1: $56.25\%$ is the total growth over two years, not the yearly rate.
optionRationale.3: $28.125\%$ divides the total growth by $2$, ignoring compounding.

questions.objective: Compute a compound annual growth rate

questions.stem: A loan of ₹5,00,000 at $9\%$ per annum is to be repaid in $60$ equal monthly instalments by the reducing balance method. Using $(1.0075)^{60} \approx 1.5657$, the EMI is closest to
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is $i = 9/12\% = 0.0075$. EMI $= P\,i(1+i)^n/[(1+i)^n - 1] = 500000 \times 0.0075 \times 1.5657/0.5657 \approx ₹10{,}379$. This is below the flat-rate instalment because interest falls as the balance reduces.

optionRationale.2: ₹12,083 is the flat-rate instalment, which charges interest on the full principal throughout.
optionRationale.3: ₹8,333 is just $5{,}00{,}000/60$ and leaves out interest altogether.
optionRationale.4: ₹8,396 adds only one month's interest to the principal before dividing by $60$.

questions.objective: Compute an EMI under the reducing balance method

questions.stem: A company must have ₹8,00,000 after $4$ years to replace a plant. It makes equal deposits at the end of each year in a sinking fund earning $10\%$ per annum compounded annually. Using $(1.1)^4 = 1.4641$, the annual deposit is closest to
questions.explanation: The future value of an annuity gives $F = R[(1+i)^n - 1]/i$, so $R = Fi/[(1+i)^n - 1] = 800000 \times 0.1/0.4641 \approx ₹1{,}72{,}377$. Interest does part of the work, so the deposit is below $8{,}00{,}000/4 = ₹2{,}00{,}000$.

optionRationale.1: ₹2,00,000 is $8{,}00{,}000/4$ and ignores the interest earned by the fund.
optionRationale.2: ₹54,641 uses $(1+i)^n$ in the denominator instead of $(1+i)^n - 1$.
optionRationale.3: ₹5,46,410 is $8{,}00{,}000/(1.1)^4$, which treats the target as one lump sum to discount rather than a series of deposits.

questions.objective: Find the periodic deposit of a sinking fund

questions.stem: Match each financial quantity in List-I with its formula in List-II.

left: A. EMI under the reducing balance method (monthly rate $i$, $n$ instalments, loan $P$)
B. Present value of a perpetuity of $C$ per period at rate $i$ per period
C. Equal periodic deposit $R$ to reach a target $F$ in $n$ periods at rate $i$
D. CAGR from value $V_i$ to value $V_f$ in $n$ years

questions.explanation: The reducing-balance EMI is $P i (1+i)^n/[(1+i)^n - 1]$ (II). A perpetuity is worth $C/i$ (I). The sinking fund deposit is $F i/[(1+i)^n - 1]$ (IV). CAGR is the $n$th root of the growth ratio minus one (III). Hence A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

optionRationale.1: Items A and B have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.
optionRationale.2: Items C and D have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.
optionRationale.4: Items A and C have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.

questions.objective: Recall the standard formulas of financial mathematics

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A bond whose coupon rate is higher than the market yield required by investors has a present value above its face value.
Reason (R): A bond repays its face value to the holder when it matures.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Take face value ₹1,000 with coupon $10\%$ and required yield $8\%$. The coupons of ₹100 exceed the $8\%$ return investors need, so discounting at $8\%$ gives a value above ₹1,000; A is true. R is also true, but repayment of face value occurs for every bond and does not explain why the price is above par; the coupon surplus does.

optionRationale.1: R is true but common to all bonds, so it cannot be what makes the price exceed the face value.
optionRationale.3: R is true: the face value is repaid at maturity.
optionRationale.4: A is true: such a bond sells at a premium.

questions.objective: Relate coupon rate, yield and bond price

questions.stem: A bond of face value ₹1,000 pays a $10\%$ annual coupon for $2$ years and is redeemed at par at the end. Investors require a yield of $8\%$ per annum. The present value (price) of the bond is closest to
questions.explanation: Price $= 100/1.08 + 1100/1.08^2 = 92.59 + 943.07 = ₹1{,}035.67$. The coupon rate exceeds the required yield, so the bond sells at a premium above ₹1,000. Always discount the final coupon together with the redemption value.

optionRationale.2: ₹1,000 would be the price only if the coupon rate equalled the required yield.
optionRationale.3: ₹964.33 would be a discount price, which needs a coupon below the yield.
optionRationale.4: ₹1,100 is the final-year cash flow, not a present value.

questions.objective: Value a bond by discounting its cash flows

questions.stem: An investment earns a nominal return of $12\%$ in a year in which inflation is $5\%$. Using the exact relation $(1 + \text{nominal}) = (1 + \text{real})(1 + \text{inflation})$, the real rate of return is closest to
questions.explanation: From the exact relation, $1 + \text{real} = 1.12/1.05 = 1.06667$, so the real return is about $6.67\%$. The simple difference $12 - 5 = 7\%$ is only an approximation and slightly overstates purchasing-power growth.

optionRationale.1: $7\%$ is the simple difference of the two rates, an approximation rather than the exact value.
optionRationale.2: $17.6\%$ results from multiplying the two growth factors instead of dividing.
optionRationale.3: $6.25\%$ divides the $7\%$ gap by $1.12$ instead of $1.05$; inflation is the deflator.

questions.objective: Compute the real rate of return from nominal return and inflation

questions.stem: A loan of ₹2,00,000 at $12\%$ per annum is repaid in $24$ equal monthly instalments (reducing balance), and the EMI works out to ₹9,414.69. How much of the first instalment goes towards reducing the principal?
questions.explanation: In the first month the interest is $200000 \times 0.01 = ₹2{,}000$ on the full balance. The rest of the instalment repays the principal: $9414.69 - 2000 = ₹7{,}414.69$. The interest share decreases and the principal share increases in later months.

optionRationale.1: ₹9,414.69 is the whole instalment, which also covers the interest.
optionRationale.2: ₹2,000 is the interest part of the first instalment, not the principal part.
optionRationale.4: ₹8,333.33 is $2{,}00{,}000/24$, the principal part under a flat plan.

questions.objective: Split an EMI into its interest and principal parts

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. For the same quoted annual rate and period, the total interest paid under the reducing balance method is less than under the flat-rate method.
B. The present value of a perpetuity falls when the rate of interest rises.
C. For a fixed target, the annual sinking-fund deposit increases when the rate of interest rises.
D. A flat-rate loan of ₹P at $r\%$ for $t$ years is repaid in equal instalments of $P(1 + rt/100)$ divided by the number of instalments.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: A is true: under reducing balance interest is charged only on the outstanding amount. B is true since $C/i$ decreases as $i$ increases. C is false: a higher rate makes the fund grow faster, so a smaller deposit is enough. D is the correct flat-rate EMI formula, so D is true.

optionRationale.1: C is false because a higher rate lowers the deposit needed, so A and C cannot be the whole truth.
optionRationale.3: C is false, and D, a correct statement, is missing here.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so the statement set that includes it cannot be correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on loans, perpetuities and sinking funds
